complaint: A 39-year-old man with an unremarkable medical history presented to our hospital.

events.t: A 39-year-old man with an unremarkable medical history presented to our hospital.
His family history was unremarkable.
At the age of 36, a load weighing more than 100 kg fell toward him while he was at work.
While attempting to catch the object, he was dragged and his body was forcibly twisted to the left.
The patient immediately developed severe neck and lower back pain, and was unable to move.

He was transported to a local emergency department, where computed tomography (CT) of the chest, abdomen, thoracic spine, and lumbar spine revealed no significant abnormalities, and he was subsequently discharged.
The following day, worsening of the posterior neck and lower back pain prompted a consultation with the orthopedic department of another hospital.
Lumbar magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed right sacral bone contusion and lumbar disc herniation.
Conservative treatment, consisting primarily of pain management and rehabilitation, was initiated.
A sacral nerve block was also performed; however, its therapeutic effect was limited.

One month post-injury, the patient developed an unexplained fever (37–38 °C), abnormal sensations and tremors involving the trunk and all four limbs, sensation of head heaviness, and severe worsening pain in the lower back.
Consequently, he was referred to a tertiary neurology department two months post-injury.
Neurological findings revealed neither muscle weakness nor abnormalities in the deep tendon reflexes.
Because of the unexplained hypertension and persistent fever, autoimmune diseases and pheochromocytoma were considered in the differential diagnosis.
However, comprehensive laboratory investigations including serum catecholamine measurements revealed no significant abnormalities.

Neurophysiological examinations, including nerve conduction studies, repetitive nerve stimulation, and somatosensory-evoked potentials of both the upper and lower extremities, revealed no abnormalities.
Autonomic function was assessed using the head-up tilt test and sympathetic skin response, neither of which revealed any abnormalities; however, heart rate variability was not assessed.
Brain MRI revealed no structural abnormalities.

Cervical MRI demonstrated mild C6/7 foraminal stenosis associated with a small C7 disc herniation without spinal cord compression, which was considered insufficient to explain the generalized movement disorder of the patient.
Since the symptoms developed after the traumatic injury and were accompanied by autonomic manifestations, Barré–Lieou syndrome was considered the most likely diagnosis.
Due to persistent hypertension, further cardiological evaluation with cardiac CT and echocardiography revealed dilated cardiomyopathy.
Sacubitril/valsartan (200 mg/day), empagliflozin (10 mg/day), and vericiguat (2.5 mg/day) were administered to treat the heart failure associated with dilated cardiomyopathy.
During follow-up at a local hospital, the patient developed a migraine that was not present before the injury.
Therefore, metoprolol (120 mg/day) and lomerizine (10 mg/day) were administered, with sumatriptan (50 mg) used as needed for acute migraine attacks.
All regularly scheduled medications were maintained at unchanged doses throughout the rTMS treatment and rehabilitation periods.
The patient also underwent prolonged rehabilitation without any significant improvement in the motor symptoms.

Subsequently, a movement disorder specialist established the diagnosis of FMD based on positive clinical signs, including marked variability, distractibility, entrainment during rhythmic tapping, co-contraction, and incongruence with known organic movement disorders.
The patient underwent cognitive behavioral therapy; however, no clinically meaningful improvement in motor symptoms was observed.
He was ultimately referred to our hospital for evaluation of eligibility for rTMS treatment.
At presentation to our hospital, generalized co-contraction was absent while the patient was seated, but became pronounced during voluntary limb movements accompanied by tremors.
Even simple elevation of both upper limbs required considerable effort and resulted in shortness of breath.
While walking, upper limb tremors were absent when the patient used a cane.
However, knee tremor, intermittent knee buckling, and excessive knee extension were observed.
The tremors showed marked variability depending on the posture and type of upper limb movement performed, which is consistent with the characteristic features of FMD.
Video 1 shows the pre-treatment recording on the left and the post-treatment recording on the right.
EEG was performed on admission and repeated after the intervention.
Resting-state EEG was recorded using a Neurofax EEG-1260 (Nihon Kohden Corp., Tokyo, Japan), with electrodes placed according to the international 10–20 system.
The averaged bilateral auricular electrodes (A1 and A2) served as references, and the ground (Z) electrode was placed at the nasion.
Recordings were acquired under eyes-closed, resting conditions using a monopolar montage (sampling rate: 200 Hz, band-pass filter: 1–45 Hz).

They lasted for approximately 6 min. After visual inspection of the continuous recording, the initial and terminal portions containing recording-related or movement artifacts were excluded, and a continuous 5-min segment with minimal artifacts was selected for subsequent analysis.
Power spectral density (PSD) and weighted phase lag index (wPLI) analyses () were performed using MNE-Python (version 1.12.1) and MNE-connectivity (version 0.7.0) ().
PSD was estimated using Welch’s method with 2-s segments and 50% overlap between adjacent segments.
The fast Fourier transform length was set equal to the segment length, yielding a frequency resolution of 0.5 Hz.
The PSD estimates obtained from individual segments were averaged arithmetically.
The resulting spectra were linearly interpolated onto a frequency grid ranging from 1.5625 to 46 Hz.

For each electrode, the PSD at each frequency was normalized by the sum of the PSD values across the analyzed frequency range to obtain the normalized PSD such that the sum of the normalized PSD values within each electrode was equal to 1.

For functional connectivity analysis, the EEG data were notch-filtered at 50 Hz and band-pass filtered between 1 and 40 Hz using zero-phase finite impulse response filters, followed by reference to the common average.
Independent component analysis was performed using the Fast algorithm with 15 components.
The components corresponding to ocular artifacts were identified using Fp1 as a surrogate electrooculography channel and removed.
Eighteen electrodes (Fz, Fp1, F3, F7, T3, C3, T5, P3, O1, O2, P4, T6, C4, T4, F8, F4, Fp2, and Cz) were selected, and the cleaned continuous EEG was divided into non-overlapping 4-s epochs.
Functional connectivity was quantified using the debiased estimator of the squared weighted phase lag index (wPLI2-debiased) with a Fourier-based spectral estimation.
Connectivity was calculated for all electrode pairs and averaged within the theta (4–8 Hz), alpha (8–13 Hz), and beta (13–30 Hz) frequency bands.
No connectivity threshold was applied to the quantitative analysis.
Given the single-case design, pre- and post-intervention EEG changes were evaluated descriptively, and inferential statistical testing was not performed.
Accordingly, corrections for multiple comparisons were not applied.
Normalized PSD analysis demonstrated increased theta-band power at Cz.
In addition, wPLI analysis revealed excessive functional connectivity centered on C4 in the alpha and beta frequency bands.

Previous functional neuroimaging studies have demonstrated reduced functional connectivity between the rTPJ, a key region involved in the sense of agency, and sensorimotor regions, including the bilateral SMA, in patients with FMD ().

Given the bilateral and widespread nature of the patient’s motor symptoms, including bilateral tremor and co-contraction, we considered the SMA as a clinically relevant target that allowed simultaneous modulation of the bilateral medial motor regions.

The scalp EEG findings, including relatively prominent theta-band activity at Cz and altered C4-centered functional connectivity, were considered supportive of motor network dysfunction but were not interpreted as directly localizing the abnormality to the SMA.
Based on these clinical, neurophysiological, and previously reported network findings, the bilateral SMA was selected as the stimulation target.
Based on this rationale, transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) was initially administered using a Compact DC Stimulator GD-800 (OG Wellness Technologies Co., Ltd., Okayama, Japan).

Assuming hyperexcitability at Cz, a 5 × 7 cm rectangular cathodal electrode was placed over Cz to suppress cortical excitability, and stimulation was delivered at 2 mA for 20 min; however, no clinical improvement was observed.
Subsequently, bilateral cathodal stimulation of the primary motor cortex (M1) was performed simultaneously using the two stimulators.
However, this approach was ineffective.
We subsequently initiated rTMS targeting the SMA using a MagPro R30 stimulator (MagVenture A/S, Farum, Denmark) based on this rationale.
The target was defined as a point 2.5 cm anterior to Cz, corresponding to the SMA.
Low-frequency rTMS was delivered at 1 Hz and 90% of the resting motor threshold, with 900 pulses administered over 15 min per session.
Treatment was performed every 2–3 days during the 2-week hospitalization for six sessions (5,400 pulses in total).
Immediately after the first rTMS session, tremors associated with bilateral upper- and lower-limb elevations were noticeably reduced on visual clinical observation.
The symptoms were quantitatively assessed using the Simplified Functional Movement Disorders Rating Scale (S-FMDRS) ().
The severity score decreased from 14/27 before stimulation to 11/27 at discharge, whereas the duration score remained unchanged at 15/27.
A reduction in tremors following rTMS was evident, but the patient showed little subjective awareness of the improvement, consistent with previous reports.
Therefore, visual feedback was provided by reviewing videos recorded before and after treatment to facilitate the recognition of clinical improvement.
The patient received 60 min of daily physical and occupational therapy during hospitalization.
During the early phase of hospitalization, excessive tremors occurred immediately after the initiation of voluntary movements, making active exercise therapy difficult.
Therefore, during the first week, rehabilitation focused primarily on relaxation techniques and management of low back pain.
From the second week onward, visual feedback using mirror-based and simple task-oriented movement exercises were gradually introduced as tolerated.

At the final assessment, tremors in both the upper and lower limbs did not completely resolve, but both the 10-m walking time (11.22 s to 8.59 s) and Timed Up and Go test time (clockwise; 13.87 s to 9.47 s) showed improvement compared with the baseline (Video 1-Right).
EEG performed immediately before discharge demonstrated modulation of alpha- and beta-band functional connectivity patterns with reduced relative prominence of the C4-centered connectivity.
In the alpha band, the mean C4 connectivity increased modestly from 0.127 to 0.150, whereas the global mean connectivity increased from 0.048 to 0.102.
Among the 17 electrode pairs involving C4, the wPLI increased for 12 pairs and decreased in 5 pairs.

Consequently, despite the increase in mean C4 connectivity, the ratio of C4 mean connectivity to global mean connectivity decreased from 2.67 to 1.46, and the C4 node-strength rank changed from first to third among the 18 electrodes.
In the beta band, the mean C4 connectivity decreased from 0.0349 to 0.0263 and the C4 node strength decreased from 0.593 to 0.448.
Among the 17 electrode pairs involving C4, wPLI increased in 6 pairs and decreased in 11 pairs.
The C4/global connectivity ratio decreased from 2.95 to 1.29, and the node strength rank changed from first to fifth.
These pairwise changes were evaluated descriptively and not subjected to inferential statistical testing.
Summary metrics of C4-centered connectivity are presented in Supplementary Table S1, and detailed pairwise wPLI values are provided in Supplementary Table S2.

At the 1-month follow-up, clinical improvements were sustained, and the patient reported improvements in activities of daily living, lower back pain, and joint pain, indicating a high level of satisfaction with the treatment.
However, the tremor recurred two months later.

pearls: Barré–Lieou syndrome is currently regarded as a historical and controversial diagnostic concept (); however, it was initially considered because of the patient’s post-traumatic neck pain and prominent autonomic symptoms.
Traditionally, FMD has been considered a psychogenic disorder.
Despite the apparent visual reduction in tremors after rTMS, the patient initially showed little subjective awareness of improvement.

However, he was able to visually recognize the improvement and became increasingly aware of the ease of performing voluntary movements after reviewing the video recordings obtained before and after treatment.

src.title: Case Report: Electroencephalography-informed low-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation targeting the supplementary motor area in severe functional movement disorder
src.authors: Chiaki Takahashi, Takashi Asahi, Motoki Kanda et al.

complaint: Patient information

events.t: Patient information
A 50-year-old male, farmer by occupation, reached out to the Physiotherapy department with symptoms of lower back discomfort for the previous two years as well as trouble completing everyday duties.
The pain was insidious in onset, gradual in progression, and mild in intensity initially but increased to moderate in the last three months.
The pain was aggravating on movement and while doing farm activities; it radiated to both the lower limbs and was associated with a tingling sensation in both lower limbs.
It was relieved on rest and with analgesic medications.
The patient had consulted at a private hospital for the above complaint where an MRI-lumbosacral spine was done.
Table 1 shows the timeline of events.
On examination, the patient was seen in the supine position with the head supported by a pillow, upper limbs by the side, and lower limbs relaxed and extended.
The patient was mesomorphic with no complications after the surgery.

Patient assessment details taken before the rehabilitation included manual muscle testing (MMT), range of motion (ROM), pain assessment by the visual analog scale (VAS), along with Oswestry Disability Index scores and functional independence measure (FIM).
Pre-rehabilitation manual muscle testing is shown in Table 2 and the pre-rehabilitation range of motion is described in Table 3.
Radiological imaging findings
Investigations using an MRI of the lumbosacral spine (lateral view) suggest kyphosis with multiple osteophytes seen at various levels.
This was suggestive of severe, multiple-level, degenerative changes.
Spinal canal stenosis at the lumbar level was also noted.
The findings were suggestive of Scheuermann disease.

Demographic information on Scheuermann disease features involves vertebral level and their numbers, amount of degenerative disc disease, and associated magnetic resonance imaging findings of patients.
Following the diagnosis, posterior decompression and spinal fixation of L3-L4 and L4-L5 were recommended.
No post-surgical complications were seen.
The patient was conservatively managed by thoracic bracing.
Physiotherapy rehabilitation
A single physical therapist devised and delivered personalized face-to-face physiotherapy to avoid any inter-rater disagreements.
Physiotherapy involved a weekly five-session adaptive program organized into four phases to treat particular deficiencies and restore independent standing and ambulatory abilities.
Rehabilitation was divided into four phases over a 12-week duration as shown in Table 4.
The duration of each phase was decided by the performance of the preceding phase's obligations.
The first phase concentrated on strengthening the extremities and core muscles to prepare for motor function.
Therapy began one week following surgery and continued throughout the program.
Workouts began in a supine posture and progressed to a standing stationary position.
In the supine position, isometric exercises were performed for the lower extremities.
Dynamic, active, assisted exercises for upper extremities were also performed.
The physiotherapy exercise protocol followed during rehabilitation is shown in Table 5.
During the second phase, aquatic equilibrium and stance training were implemented to adapt to the upright posture.
Surgical incisions had healed sufficiently for safe water exposure during the second phase, which began around a month following surgery.
Aquatic therapy was recommended over terrestrial training because it reduced axial stress on the spine.
The focus of the second phase was on promoting standing and movement.
Each day, a session was conducted for a period of five weeks.
The primary objective was to enhance the duration of standing while minimizing the need for assistance.
Patients in the third phase underwent gait training to prepare for the physical demands of walking.
Gait training consists of tandem walking, walking sideways, using the parallel bar, and treadmill training.
This enhances muscle memory, which improves walking.
The patient has to be able to stand for at least 10 seconds, either with or without help.
The fourth phase is based on sit-to-stance training.
Outcome measures
Outcomes were measured pre- and post-rehabilitation by the physical therapist.
The visual analog scale score while exercising decreased from 6/10 to 2/10 following rehabilitation.
Furthermore, Oswestry Disability Index scores were compared before and after rehabilitation.
A clinical study of Oswestry Disability Index data demonstrates a good impact of the rehabilitation program.
The patient's strength was evaluated before surgery and at the end of the fourth phase by evaluating the muscles related to their lumbar and sacral nerve roots.
Strength was tested using the Medical Research Council Scale for Muscle Strength, which ranges from 0 to 5+and the results showed an improvement.
Furthermore, the range of motion of the hip joint was recorded using goniometry, and improvements were observed in post-rehabilitation.
Functional independence measures properly analyze a person's limitations in self-care, sphincter control, mobility, and locomotion.
This was used to assess each patient before surgery and at the end of the fourth phase of rehabilitation.
Table 8 shows the outcome measure scales in evaluation metrics.

pearls: In the interim, the administration of medications and participation in physiotherapy are crucial components of the treatment process.
Sports that involve exerting significant pressure on the spine like weightlifting as well as those that subject the vertebra to repetitive stress, such as rugby, should always be avoided.

Collaboration among physiotherapists, orthopedic surgeons, and other healthcare professionals from different disciplines is crucial for creating personalized treatment plans and ensuring a smooth continuum of care.
Education and guidance on correct body mechanics, posture, and adjusting activities are essential elements of rehabilitation.

Overall physiotherapy rehabilitation plays an essential role in the overall care of Scheuermann's illness and postoperative lumbar spine disease, aiding in functional restoration, enhancing quality of life, and encouraging long-term spinal health.

src.title: A Holistic Approach to Physiotherapy Treatment for Scheuermann Disease Along With Lumbar Canal Stenosis and Bilateral Lower Limb Radiculopathy: A Case Report
src.authors: Pradhyum D Kolhe, Nikita G Zanwar, Pratik Phansopkar

complaint: A 49-year-old Asian woman presented with recurrent vomiting in September 2020.

events.t: A 49-year-old Asian woman presented with recurrent vomiting in September 2020.
Spinal cord magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed no obvious abnormality of the cervical or thoracic spinal cord.
Brain MRI demonstrated abnormal lesions in the medulla oblongata, bilateral hypothalamus, and white matter of the cerebral hemispheres.
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed positive oligoclonal IgG bands (OCBs).
Her tests for AQP4-IgG in CSF (1:1) and serum (1:10) were positive, confirming the diagnosis of NMOSD.
Her muscle strength of left upper and lower limbs were rated 5− level and her right limbs were normal.
Her muscular tension were normal but tendon reflex was active.
Her binocular diplopia and distal vision decreased.
Also, the pharyngeal reflex was disappeared.
During September 2020 to the end of February 2021, she lived at local hospital and ate mycophenolate mofetil dispersible tablets 0.75 mg bid and prednisone 20 mg qd.
At the end of February 2021, the overall situation has improved.
Her strength of limbs and tendon reflex return back to normal level.
Her pharyngeal reflex was weakened.
Her binocular diplopia was alleviated, and distal vision decreased slightly.

Then she visited the neurology outpatient department of our hospital on 1 April, 2021, the attending doctor adjusted the dose of prednisone to 15 mg qd and mycophenolate mofetil dispersible tablets 0.75 mg bid.
She went to the neurology clinic again in June.
Given the stability of the condition, the doctor reduced the dose of prednisone to 10 mg qod and mycophenolate mofetil dispersible tablets 0.75 mg bid until now.
However, the dysphagia persisted even after the immunotherapy treatment.
Consequently, she presented to our department in 23 March 2021 for further intervention.
Initially, a videofluoroscopic swallowing study (VFSS) indicated that she has an aspiration and her UES was not opening on swallowing 3 ml of an extremely thick bolus (Softia-S, Nutri.
Co., Ltd., Japan).
The first fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing (FEES) revealed moderate residue in the epiglottis valley and piriform sinus ().
Her functional oral intake scale (FOIS) score was 1 ().
On high-resolution pharyngeal manometry (HRPM), the upper esophageal sphincter (UES) residue pressure was 259.5 mmHg when she swallowed 3 ml of an extremely thick bolus.
The normal reference value for UES residual pressure is <12 mmHg (), this patients' UES residue pressure was higher than the normal range.
The VFSS and HRPM results represented that she had cricopharyngeal muscle (CPM) dysfunction.
Hence, the speech-language pathologist (SLP) treated her with catheter balloon dilation.
However, her swallowing function failed to improve after 2 weeks of training.

Since the botulinum toxin (BTX) relieves muscle tone, the clinician decided to inject her CPM with 50 U of onabotulinum toxin A (Botox®, Irvine, CA, USA), diluted to 100 U/ml with normal saline, under the combined guidance of a catheter balloon, ultrasound, and electromyography (BECURE).
After the first injection, her UES residue pressure was still higher than normal (151.9 mmHg).
Considering that the dosage was insufficient, another 50 U of BTX was injected into the CPM ().
Her swallowing dysfunction persisted despite 2 weeks of training.
Fifteen days after the second injection, her UES residue pressure remained high (74.0 mmHg) and she could not eat.
The clinicians deemed it safe and necessary to administer the third dose of 50 U of BTX into the CPM.
Sixteen days after the third injection, the patient's UES residue pressure further decreased to 47.5 mmHg.
And the VFSS results showed that her UES were opening without aspiration.
She was able to eat 100 ml of extremely thick food and spit out 20 ml.
At the 6- and 9-month follow-ups after the last injection, she could consume an unlimited variety of foods orally.

pearls: For these patients, BTX injection into the CPM may be considered.
Beside the location, the dosage of BTX is also important.
Consider the above information comprehensively, we decided to inject 50 U diluted in 0.5 ml normal saline to this patient.
The main considerations were to reduce side effects and have effects.

Patients can eat when A + B ≥ C. This complex series of movements is considered to be controlled by medullary swallowing center, which is called swallowing central pattern generators (CPG), especially the neucleus of the solitary tract (NTS) and other medullary or supra-medullary structure ().

src.title: Botulinum toxin injection combined with traditional swallowing rehabilitation improved cricopharyngeal dysfunction in neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder: A case report
src.authors: Zitong He, Fei Zhao, Yilong Shan et al.

complaint: A 33-year-old man with obesity, hypertension, obstructive sleep apnea, and depression, who had previously been independent in activities of daily living, developed progressive bilateral lower-extremity weakness, impaired ambulation, sensory disturbance, and declining functional independence in the setting of severe thoracic spinal stenosis.

events.t: A 33-year-old man with obesity, hypertension, obstructive sleep apnea, and depression, who had previously been independent in activities of daily living, developed progressive bilateral lower-extremity weakness, impaired ambulation, sensory disturbance, and declining functional independence in the setting of severe thoracic spinal stenosis.
Before the initial surgical intervention, the available neurological examination documented 5/5 upper-extremity strength with bilateral lower-extremity weakness in the approximately 4/5 range.
Sensation was impaired below a thoracic level, and hyperreflexia and other findings consistent with thoracic myelopathy were documented.
Gait was impaired, while bowel and bladder function remained preserved.

A complete segment-by-segment ISNCSCI examination and formal preoperative AIS classification were not documented; therefore, a preoperative lower-extremity motor score could not be reliably calculated.
The patient underwent T1-T2 laminectomy and facetectomy for decompression, posterior fusion, and instrumentation on February 4, 2026.
He was subsequently admitted to inpatient rehabilitation on February 9.
On February 11, he developed progressive left-greater-than-right lower-extremity weakness with a new left foot drop and worsening gait impairment, ultimately becoming unable to ambulate.
Further evaluation identified multilevel thoracic disc herniation with severe spinal cord compression.
The patient was transferred back to acute care and subsequently underwent T1-T7 posterior bilateral instrumented fusion and laminectomies on February 14, 2026.
Representative postoperative CT imaging obtained after the initial T1-T2 procedure and before the subsequent T1-T7 operation demonstrated upper thoracic instrumentation.
Preoperative imaging and imaging obtained after the final T1-T7 posterior fusion and laminectomies were not available for inclusion.
Following medical stabilization, the patient was readmitted to inpatient rehabilitation on February 22, 2026.
At that time, the injury was documented as T10 AIS C. Upper-extremity strength was 5/5 throughout.
In the right lower extremity, hip flexion was 2/5, knee extension was 3/5, and ankle dorsiflexion was 3/5.
In the left lower extremity, hip flexion was 2/5, knee extension was 2/5, and ankle dorsiflexion was 1/5.
Light-touch sensation was reduced in the lower extremities and below approximately the T10 level.
Lower-extremity tone was documented as normal, clonus was absent, and Babinski responses were negative.
The patient was unable to ambulate.
The T10 designation represents the clinical neurological level and is distinct from the vertebral levels addressed surgically.
Vertebral levels of compression, decompression, and instrumentation do not directly determine the neurological level of injury.

Although the rehabilitation documentation classified the injury as T10 AIS C, the original formal ISNCSCI worksheet and complete motor and sensory subscores were unavailable for independent reconstruction.
In addition, great-toe extension and ankle plantarflexion grades were not available in the admission examination; therefore, a complete lower-extremity motor score could not be calculated.
Rehabilitation course
The patient was admitted to inpatient rehabilitation on February 22, 2026, eight days after the second surgical procedure.

His rehabilitation program included at least three hours of combined physical and occupational therapy on treatment days, with a weekly minimum of approximately 15 hours of therapy, in addition to 24-hour specialized rehabilitation nursing care under physiatry supervision.

Physical therapy emphasized bed mobility, transfer training, seated and standing balance, trunk control, progressive standing tolerance, strengthening and motor-control activities, wheelchair mobility, and overground gait training with a front-wheeled walker.
Occupational therapy emphasized functional transfers, dressing, bathing, toileting, upper-extremity conditioning, adaptive strategies, and task-specific activities-of-daily-living retraining.
Rehabilitation nursing and case management addressed medical monitoring, skin protection, pain management, caregiver education, safety, and discharge planning.
Initial functional status at rehabilitation admission
At admission and during the early rehabilitation period, the patient was non-ambulatory and required moderate to maximal assistance for bed mobility and total or two-person assistance for transfers.
Lower-extremity weakness, impaired motor control, poor balance, and his body habitus significantly limited mobility.
He was dependent for wheelchair mobility, lower-body dressing, and toileting and required maximal assistance for bathing and upper-body dressing.
The neurological and functional findings together demonstrated substantial impairment at the beginning of the rehabilitation course.

However, neurological impairment and functional dependence were considered separately throughout this report because assistance levels are influenced not only by muscle strength and sensation but also by balance, endurance, pain, fear of falling, compensatory strategies, and task-specific performance.
Early rehabilitation phase: week 1
During the first week, treatment focused on bed mobility, transfer training, seated balance, trunk control, and supported standing tolerance.
The patient demonstrated progressive improvement in trunk control and required less assistance with bed mobility and transfers.
Standing activities were introduced with substantial assistance.
Gait training was initially deferred because of limited lower-extremity activation, impaired motor control, and insufficient stability for safe stepping.
Intermediate rehabilitation phase: weeks 2-3
As therapy progressed, the patient demonstrated improved lower-extremity activation, motor control, supported-standing tolerance, and knee stability.
These clinical changes allowed initiation of assisted overground gait training with a front-wheeled walker.
He initially ambulated approximately 50-70 feet with assistance.
Transfers progressed to minimal assistance, and wheelchair mobility improved substantially.
Functional gains were also observed in dressing and bathing, with assistance levels decreasing from maximal or dependent levels toward moderate and minimal assistance.

Formal muscle-strength, trunk-control, or balance-score thresholds used to determine readiness for gait training were not documented; initiation and progression were based on the treating therapists’ clinical assessment of strength, motor control, stability, standing tolerance, and safety.
Late rehabilitation phase: final week prior to discharge
During the final week, the patient continued to improve in mobility, coordination, endurance, and independence.
He progressed to contact guard assistance for transfers and assisted ambulation.
Gait distance increased to 170 feet using a front-wheeled walker with contact guard assistance.
Wheelchair mobility improved to approximately 150 feet with standby assistance.
Activities of daily living also improved.
The patient became independent with eating, required supervision for upper-body dressing, and required minimal assistance for lower-body dressing and bathing.
Fear of falling remained an important barrier during portions of the rehabilitation course.

It intermittently affected confidence and willingness to participate in challenging mobility activities but improved with graded exposure, repetition, successful task completion, and therapist guidance.
Functional status at discharge
At discharge on March 20, 2026, the patient performed bed mobility with standby assistance and transfers with contact guard assistance using a front-wheeled walker.
He completed assisted ambulation of 170 feet with a front-wheeled walker and contact guard assistance.
He was discharged home with home health services, family support, caregiver education, and training after a total inpatient rehabilitation stay of 26 days.
Table 1 shows the functional progression during inpatient rehabilitation.

Standardized neurological and rehabilitation outcome measures, including serial ISNCSCI motor and sensory subscores, lower extremity motor scores, Trunk Control Test for Spinal Cord Injury, Spinal Cord Independence Measure III, Functional Independence Measure, Walking Index for Spinal Cord Injury II, Berg Balance Scale, 10-Meter Walk Test, and Six-Minute Walk Test, were not available and were not retrospectively inferred.

pearls: The preoperative neurological examination provides important context for interpreting this trajectory.

After the definitive T1-T7 decompression and stabilization, the rehabilitation-admission examination continued to demonstrate substantial asymmetric lower-extremity paresis, with strength ranging from 1/5 to 3/5 in the documented key muscle groups.
The principal longitudinal outcome demonstrated in this case is therefore functional recovery, while the neurological examinations serve as important clinical context.

Tamai et al. reported frequent AIS conversion among patients with AIS C SCI, while Stenimahitis et al. identified baseline AIS grade and lower-extremity motor function as important predictors of later ambulation.

More recent prognostic evidence likewise identifies baseline neurological severity, neurological level, and motor function as important determinants of walking recovery, although much of this literature is derived from traumatic SCI populations.

src.title: Early Functional Improvement in American Spinal Injury Association Impairment Scale Grade C (AIS C) Non-Traumatic Spinal Cord Injury Following Staged Thoracic Decompression and Inpatient Rehabilitation: A Case Report
src.authors: Ramiz K Ahmed, Sarah Shandy, Harjas Jassal et al.

complaint: A 17-year-old male patient reported an asymptomatic swelling with a four-year evolution.

events.t: A 17-year-old male patient reported an asymptomatic swelling with a four-year evolution.
On extraoral physical examination, facial asymmetry was observed due to expansive growth involving the symphysis and left mandibular body, painless on palpation.
On intraoral examination, there was effacement of the gingival-labial sulcus with buccal and lingual bulging and displacement of the mandibular anterior teeth.

In the panoramic radiography, it was possible to observe a radiolucent and multilocular image, extending from the right mandibular body to the left mandibular ramus and from the alveolar bone crest to the base of the mandible, causing deformity and discontinuity.
Tooth displacement and inclusion of the mandibular left canine in the tumor mass were also noted.

On computed tomography, coronal and axial sections, an extensive mandibular lesion with a hypoattenuating aspect in relation to the musculature and the presence of delicate bone trabeculae was observed, causing fenestration in the basal cortex, bulging and expansion of the buccal cortex and preservation of part of the lingual cortex.
The diagnostic hypotheses were odontogenic myxoma and conventional ameloblastoma.

An incisional biopsy was performed, which demonstrated myxomatous proliferation infiltrating the bone trabeculae composed of organized stellate fusiform cells establishing the diagnosis of odontogenic myxoma.

Despite the primary indication for mandibular resection for standard treatment of the case, due to the impossibility of adequate reconstruction for this type of defect and for the preservation, even if exiguous, of parts of the lingual and basal cortex, we opted for the excision of the lesion by intraoral access.

The patient was submitted to general anesthesia, nasotracheal intubation, intrasulcular access and relaxant with a number 15 scalpel blade, mucoperiosteal detachment, maintaining the plane of separation between the lesion and the submucosal tissue, vestibular ostectomy to access the entire lesion, excision of the lesion and the teeth involved, curettage and peripheral ostectomy, followed by suturing of the mucosa.
After three years of follow-up, bone remodeling was observed with well-circumscribed unilocular images, predominantly in the left basilar region, suggestive of residual lesion.
As a result, a new surgical procedure was programmed to remove the lesion, improve the facial contour, and attempt to increase bone thickness with an iliac crest graft.
However, there were signs of contamination and non-incorporation of the graft, which was removed after 40 days, under local anesthesia.
After 120 months of follow-up, showing signs of bone remodeling and no recurrence of the lesion, it was proposed to install osseointegrated implants and a protocol-type prosthesis.
Restoring masticatory, phonetic and aesthetic functions in a more adequate way.

pearls: For young patients, conservative treatment can be adopted as a first-line treatment modality for OM, however, follow-up of patients with OM should be prolonged, especially in the first two years ().
The evolution of the case showed that this reconstruction was not essential, not even to enable implant placement.

Mandibular defects in patients who underwent resections cause severe bone and soft tissue deformities, with their consequent esthetic and functional sequelae, therefore, immediate mandibular reconstruction is recommended.

Thus, conservative treatment, when possible, is a way of helping the patient to treat the disease, maintaining facial contour, occlusal stability and maintaining as many important structures as possible for aesthetics and orofacial function ().
Careful surgical technique and learning curve are essential for the treatment of patients with this approach ().

complaint: The proband is a seven-year-old boy and the first child of healthy, non-consanguineous parents.

events.t: The proband is a seven-year-old boy and the first child of healthy, non-consanguineous parents.
His mother was a 33-year-old Middle Eastern woman with no significant past medical history, while his father was a healthy 34-year-old Native American man.
The family history was unremarkable for congenital anomalies, neurodevelopmental disorders, recurrent pregnancy loss, or known chromosomal abnormalities.
The pregnancy course was without complications until 26 weeks of gestation, when routine obstetric ultrasonography demonstrated severe IUGR associated with marked oligohydramnios.
Given the abnormal prenatal findings, amniocentesis was performed for genetic evaluation.
Chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) identified a 6.83-Mb duplication involving chromosome 19p13.3–p13.2, reported as arr [GRCh37]19p13.3p13.2 (260,911_7,089,557)x3.
Conventional fetal cytogenetic analysis with fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) demonstrated an unbalanced derivative chromosome 13 inherited from the mother and was reported as.
Parental chromosome studies subsequently identified a balanced reciprocal translocation in the mother.
The fetal and maternal karyotypes are shown in Figures 1, 2, respectively.
The fetal chromosomal imbalance was therefore interpreted as partial trisomy of chromosome 19p13.3–p13.2 resulting from maternal transmission of an unbalanced derivative chromosome 13.
The duplicated segment identified by chromosomal microarray corresponded to the additional chromosomal material detected by conventional cytogenetic analysis.
No clinically significant loss of chromosome 13 material was detected, indicating that the patient’s genomic imbalance was limited to duplication of chromosome 19p13.3–p13.2.
A summary of the genetic characterization methods is provided in Supplementary Data sheet.
Following comprehensive genetic counseling, the antenatal findings, anticipated clinical uncertainties, and available pregnancy management options were discussed with the family.
After careful consideration and in accordance with their personal values and beliefs, the parents elected to continue the pregnancy.
The pregnancy was subsequently monitored with serial ultrasonographic assessments, which demonstrated persistent fetal growth restriction throughout the remainder of the pregnancy.
The umbilical cord was also noted to contain a single umbilical artery.
The infant was delivered spontaneously at 38 weeks of gestation.
Birth weight was 1,110 g, consistent with severe growth restriction.
The Apgar score was 7 at 1 minute.
Shortly after birth, he developed respiratory distress requiring high-flow nasal cannula support and nasogastric tube feeding.
Placental examination demonstrated reduced placental size with otherwise normal morphology.
The neonate was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU), where he remained for close monitoring for 11 days before being discharged home with ongoing multidisciplinary follow-up.

Physical examination at birth demonstrated severe growth restriction with microcephaly, enlarged, soft, and full fontanelles, sparse and arched eyebrows, hypertelorism with upslanting palpebral fissures, low-set ears, a prominent nose with low-hanging columella, a long smooth philtrum with thin lips, and mild microretrognathia.
Cranial ultrasonography identified a small left choroid plexus cyst without additional structural brain parenchymal abnormalities.
The cyst resolved spontaneously by 6 months of age.
Newborn hearing screening was abnormal, and confirmatory auditory brainstem response testing performed 2 weeks later demonstrated mild-to-moderate bilateral conductive hearing loss.
Renal ultrasonography demonstrated mild left-sided hydronephrosis.
Voiding cystourethrography subsequently identified vesicoureteral reflux (grade III on the left and grade I on the right).
Cardiac evaluation by echocardiography revealed no structural cardiac abnormalities.
Feeding difficulties were evident immediately after birth and persisted beyond the neonatal period.
Nasogastric tube feeding continued throughout the NICU admission and for approximately 2 months after discharge.
Despite gradual improvement in oral intake, the patient continued to experience dysphagia with both solids and liquids, confirmed by a formal swallowing assessment.
Gastroesophageal reflux disease developed during infancy and was managed with metoclopramide therapy for approximately 2 years.

During early childhood, the patient experienced recurrent episodes of febrile seizures beginning in infancy and continuing until approximately 5 years of age, resulting in multiple hospital admissions.
Serial electroencephalograms (EEGs) remained normal, and long-term antiseizure medication was not indicated.
At 4 years of age, mild lower-limb spasticity became clinically apparent.
Further evaluation with brain magnetic resonance imaging and computed tomography showed no structural brain abnormalities.
Persistent sleep disturbances were also reported despite normal polysomnography.
The patient experienced recurrent otitis media requiring tympanostomy tube insertion and subsequently developed chronic otomycosis.
At 4 years of age, clinical examination identified a soft cleft palate associated with a bifid uvula.
Orthopedic evaluation demonstrated bilateral positional congenital foot deformities, which were successfully corrected using orthotic management over a 3-year period.
The patient also experienced recurrent urinary tract infections during early childhood.
Vesicoureteral reflux and hydronephrosis resolved spontaneously by 3 years of age, and urinary tract infections became less frequent following circumcision.
Global developmental delay became apparent during infancy and affected all developmental domains.
Gross motor development was markedly delayed.
Head control was achieved at approximately 5 months of age, independent sitting at 16 months, rolling from prone to supine at 18 months, and independent walking at 3 years of age.
Fine motor skills were also delayed.
The patient was able to reach and transfer objects at approximately 9 months of age but has yet to develop a mature pincer grasp.
Language development remains profoundly impaired.
At 7 years of age, he continues to vocalize and babble during play but has not developed intelligible speech.
Communication is primarily nonverbal, relying on gestures, such as pointing, to express his needs.
Social development is also significantly affected.

He demonstrates poor eye contact, inconsistent responses to caregivers, limited comprehension of verbal commands, and frequent behavioral outbursts, including episodes of head banging when frustrated or attempting to communicate.

At the most recent clinical assessment, the patient remained significantly developmentally delayed and fully dependent on his caregivers for activities of daily living, including feeding, dressing, hygiene, and toileting.
His growth parameters remained markedly reduced, with weight, height, and head circumference all below the 3rd centile.
Physical examination demonstrated persistent microcephaly with a relatively broad forehead and dysmorphic craniofacial features.

These included arched eyebrows, hypertelorism with upslanting palpebral fissures, intermittent esotropia, a broad nasal bridge with a prominent nasal tip and low-hanging columella, prominent low-set ears, a long smooth philtrum, a thin upper vermilion border, and mild microretrognathia.
No clinical photographs are included, in accordance with parental preference.
Neurological examination showed axial hypotonia with mild appendicular spasticity.
He was ambulatory but had significant global developmental delay, most prominently affecting expressive language, adaptive functioning, and social communication.
He remained nonverbal and communicated primarily through gestures to his caregivers.
The remainder of the systemic examination was unremarkable.
He continues to receive multidisciplinary follow-up, including speech and language pathology, occupational rehabilitation, and physiotherapy.

pearls: Neurological manifestations also varied considerably among reported patients.

Distinguishing recurrent febrile seizures from epilepsy is clinically relevant because the available literature suggests that seizure disorders are variable rather than universal manifestations of chromosome 19p duplication, and the neurological prognosis should therefore be individualized according to each patient’s clinical course rather than inferred solely from the chromosomal abnormality.

These findings suggest that clinical severity should be interpreted in the context of gene content, chromosomal breakpoint location, rearrangement mechanism, inheritance pattern, and additional genetic or environmental modifiers.
DECIPHER considers values ≥ 0.68 to correspond to a predicted odds ratio of at least 2, while values ≥ 0.94 correspond to a predicted odds ratio of at least 2.7.
Nevertheless, several limitations should be considered when interpreting these candidate genes.

src.title: Partial trisomy 19p13.3-p13.2 from antenatal diagnosis to 7-year follow-up: case report and literature review
src.authors: Reema Abualnaja, Zohor Azher, Sarah Alkhaifi et al.

complaint: A 39-year-old male (height of 175.3 and weight 98.9kg) drove a full-sized pick-up.

events.t: A 39-year-old male (height of 175.3 and weight 98.9kg) drove a full-sized pick-up.
He was stopped at an intersection when he was struck from behind by a similarly sized vehicle.
The collision caught the patient unaware, and he reported being violently thrown forward against the seat belt and then violently thrown backward into the seat.
The airbag did not deploy on the target vehicle; it is unknown if the airbag was deployed in the bullet vehicle.
He reported the NP and HA to the scene's emergency medical services (EMS).
Throughout the next few hours, his symptoms worsened, and he sought evaluation at the emergency room (ER).
Following an examination and no imaging, he was diagnosed with cervical sprain/strain and was prescribed multiple medications.
The medications prescribed were Norco, Ibuprofen, Lidoderm patch, Robaxin, and Tylenol.

His most debilitating symptom was severe migraine HA that did not relent for five days and was diagnosed by his general practitioner, who referred him to a Gillette, Wyoming, USA facility for spine rehabilitation.

At initial rehabilitation, the assessment included history, orthopedic tests, neurological testing, balance assessment, and grip strength, measured along with visual range of motion (ROM) for pain and full-spine upright radiography.
The patient reported near-constant head pain measured on the HDI (98/100), indicating severe disability.
Constant NP-causing disability found using the NDI (64/100) indicated severe disability.
The patient reported the NP radiated into the right trapezius and right arm.
The radiating pain was associated with numbness and tingling and caused weakness in the right arm.
The patient also reported LBP measured on the RODI (26/50), indicating severe disability.
QVAS for pain was assessed for cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine pain (67/100, 37/100, and 13/100, respectively), indicating moderate to severe spine pain.
Rand short-form thirty-six question (SF-36) health status questionnaire found multiple deficits compared to normative data.

The questionnaire found general health perception was reduced (35/100), physical function deficit due to pain (35/100), physical ability due to (0/100), emotional deficit due to pain was normal (100/100), social deficit was severe due to pain (0/10), and mental health deficit due to pain (32/100), and energy/fatigue due to pain (15/100).
Combined, these measures demonstrated a severe reduction in HRQoL due to the pain and suffering since this crash.
Cervical compression pain provocation testing was found to be positive for local NP, and radiating radicular pain and cervical distraction testing gave the patient temporary pain reduction.
Grip strength testing found a deficit on the right (90lbs/119.7lbs), while the grip on the non-radicular left side found no deficit.
Single leg standing balance test found 3 seconds sustained with eyes closed on the left leg and 4 seconds on the right.
This is significantly reduced for the patient's age (normal 14s for 39 old).
Visual ROM for pain assessment in the cervical spine found restriction and pain with flexion, extension, and right and left lateral flexion.
Cervical rotation was restricted but not as painful.
Radiographic full spine analysis was performed using PostureRay® (Trinity, FL, USA).
This repeatable, reliable system uses machine learning intelligence to assess intersegmental relative rotation angles (RRA), as well as absolute rotation angles (ARA) of global regions.

The patient demonstrated significant loss of cervical lordosis ARA (C2-C7 -28.0°) (-42° is ideal), and intersegmental RRA demonstrated flexion kyphotic deformity C3/C4 3.3° (-8.0° is ideal), C4/C5 2.7° (-8.0° is ideal), and significant increase compared to normal extension at C6/C7 -22.8° (-8.0° is ideal).
The atlas plane line (APL) was dramatically reduced and flexed, showing 87.9% loss of normal position -3.5° (-29.0° is ideal).
Substantial anterior head translation (AHT) was measured (+TzH /forward translation of the head along the z-axis) at 24.0mm (0.0mm is ideal).
Following the initial evaluation, the patient was found to have trauma-induced snap-through buckling consistent with MVC and pain diagnoses for cervical, thoracic, and lumbar regions.
The patient was provided informed consent and initiated treatment for his abnormal spine conditions and pain (Fig 1).
CBP® therapy consists of Mirror Image® (MI) exercises designed to strengthen postural muscles and specifically used to improve the abnormal spine configuration as demonstrated on the radiographs.

Specific exercises to increase the cervical musculature in extension were prescribed, and the ProLordotic™ (Circular Traction LLC., Huntington Beach, CA, USA) neck exercises were used while under WBV using the Power Plate® WBV device (Power Plate USA, Northbrook IL., USA).
Exercises were performed at repetitions of 5 seconds with 2 seconds rest in between for 2 minutes.
Seated thoracic extension exercises were performed on the Power Plate® for 2 minutes per treatment session.
MI® traction was utilized and consisted of a seated position with the head in slight extension while a distraction force was applied.
A secondary force was placed in the mid-cervical spine, pulling from posterior to anterior (P-A), and the patient's ribcage was stabilized.
The patient progressed through weight and time, starting at 8 minutes and working up to 20 minutes with 10 lbs in the distraction force and 25 lbs on the P-A load.
Additionally, spinal manipulative therapy (SMT) was used to reduce pain and increase ROM, and specific postural MI® SMT was used to improve postural position.
The patient was instructed to perform the postural exercises at home daily.
He was a very compliant in-office patient and reported performing his home care exercises consistently.
The patient was seen in the office three times per week for eight weeks, followed by a re-assessment of all outcome measures.
Following the twenty-four treatments, the patient was given at least a twenty-four-hour rest before re-assessment to ensure accurate results.
Symptomatic improvement was stark, and the patient was very satisfied with the treatment results.

He reported that due to the treatment, his migraine headaches were improved by 80%, neck pain, and stiffness were improved by 80%, and radicular shoulder and right arm pain, numbness, and tingling were reported to be 70% improved.
Thoracic pain was improved by 30%.
Interestingly, he reported that his anxiety and irritability were 80% improved.
Postural improvement found no coronal abnormalities, and only slight head extension (-RxH or extension rotation of the head around the x-axis) was visualized.
No positive orthopedic tests were found.
Grip strength improved dramatically to 110 lbs on the right and is now measured within normal limits (WNL).
Balance improved, and the patient could now stand for 9s on the left and 13s on the right.
All cervical and lumbar ROM was WNL without pain.
He reported cessation of all of the OTC medications.
Radiography found a significant increase in cervical lordosis from -28° to -51.1° with no kyphotic segments measured, and AHT reduced from 24mm to 8mm.
APL measured as normalized (-29.2°/-29°) (Fig 2).
HRQoL measures demonstrated multiple improvements across all regions.
HDI improved from 98/100 initially to 24/100 at re-examination.
NDI measured from 64/100 at the initial examination to 12/100.
RODI improved from 26/100 to 14/100.
QVAS improved in all regions correlated to symptom reduction.
Neck QVAS measured 17/100 at re-exam compared to 67/100 initially, thoracic QVAS improved from 37/100 to 20/100, and lumbar QVAS measured 7/100 compared to 13/100 initially.
As QVAS minimally important clinical difference (MCID) is reported as 20/100, the patient demonstrated an overall MCID for this QVAS as a significant 3.5.

SF36 was improved in all categories, with health perception (77/100), physical functioning (90/100), physical performance detriment due to pain (75/100), social function improved to 75/100, mental health (80/100), bodily pain 78/100, and energy/fatigue (65/100).
This dramatic improvement in HRQoL and patient-reported outcomes (PROs) demonstrates subjective and objective improvements and continued improvement in spinal and postural alignment.
The patient was instructed to continue to perform his home exercises and seek care if his symptoms return or if there is another exacerbation or injury.
At 10-month follow-up, the patient was contacted for re-assessment.
He reported diligent home application of postural exercises and did not report any new injuries or exacerbations.
He reported his symptoms had remained nearly resolved and continued to improve over time.
He reported not being on any medications at follow-up.
Headaches remained 80% improved from baseline.
NP and stiffness were 90% improved from the initial evaluation; radicular pain, numbness, and tingling remained 80% improved.
Thoracic spine pain was 40% improved from the initial assessment.
Anxiety and irritability continued to improve and were reported to be 90% better than baseline.
These are self-reported values; however, they correspond very well with the objective outcome measures recorded and presented in the table above.
No postural abnormalities were found.
No positive orthopedic and neurological tests were found.
ROM assessment for pain was all WNL and pain-free.
Grip strength assessment found normal strength at 114lbs on the right and 113lbs on the left.

Single leg balance assessment with eyes closed found the patient could hold the posture for 10s on the left and 11s on the right, indicating near normal balance compared to baseline initial assessment using normative data.
Upright spine radiography found the lordosis was still well maintained (C2-C7 -42.5°/42.0°).
APL moved slightly back toward baseline (-20.9°/29.0°).
No kyphotic segments were observed (Fig 3).
HDI showed continued improvement (12/100), as did NDI (12/100).
Cervical thoracic and lumbar QVAS were all found to be very mild (10/100).
RODI showed continued improvement (12/50).
All SF36 scores were at or above normal and matched normative data.
The patient was very satisfied with his results long-term and was instructed to continue his home care and seek treatment if his condition worsened.

pearls: Prescription MI® traction in the mirror image of the abnormal spine configuration begins very gently and in consideration of tolerance and progresses while maintaining the patient in a position that increases lordosis and lessens abnormal loading.
Future meta-analyses and larger clinical trials are necessary and should be funded to confirm the benefits of structural rehabilitation on injured patients.

Single-subject case reports may seem trivial, but they are crucial in understanding the foundations of intervening with any patient's conditions and the individual patient needs that must be met at that time.

src.title: Subjective and Objective Improvement in a 39-Year-Old Male Suffering From Severe Chronic Pain and Disability Using Chiropractic BioPhysics® Protocols Following Rear-Impact Motor Vehicle Crash With a 10-Month Long-Term Follow-Up
src.authors: Paul A Oakley, Jason W Haas, Thomas Woodham et al.

complaint: A 38-year-old female patient presented to the emergency room (ER) on 26th August 2019 with generalized hives (wheals), pruritus, and palpitations.

events.t: A 38-year-old female patient presented to the emergency room (ER) on 26th August 2019 with generalized hives (wheals), pruritus, and palpitations.
The patient was light-headed and dizzy, and unable to stand.
These signs and symptoms had started after a 30-minute fast walk.
There was no breathing difficulty, cough, wheezing, chest tightness, or gastrointestinal complaints, but her systolic blood pressure (BP) was 50 mmHg.
She was, therefore, treated for anaphylaxis with 0.3 mg of intramuscular epinephrine, 50 mg of intramuscular diphenhydramine, 200 mg intravenous hydrocortisone, and 2 liters of normal saline.

She responded well to this treatment and was discharged with 0.3 mg IM epinephrine autoinjector for use as needed during new attacks, advised to use fexofenadine 180 mg and oral prednisone 50 mg daily for 5 days, and referred to our allergy outpatient clinic for further evaluation.

When we assessed the patient, she reported 2 similar episodes in the last 6 months, one was on April 2019 after 20 min of running, and the other was on July 2019 after climbing stairs to the 6th floor.
None of her episodes were preceded by eating food, taking NSAIDs, or alcohol intake, and there was no relation to her menstrual period.
The patient never had asthma, rhinitis, or food allergy.
Her family history of EIA was negative.
Laboratory investigations showed normal results, including complete blood count and differential, renal and liver functions, thyroid function, c-reactive protein, spirometry, and chest x-ray.

Baseline serum tryptase was 4.4 ng/ml, total IgE was 26 IU/ml, and blood tests for specific IgE to common foods, including milk, wheat, peanut, tree nuts, fish, shellfish, egg, soybeans, sesame, and legumes and common inhaled allergens as well as latex were all negative.

Based on that, the patient was diagnosed with EIA and advised to avoid strenuous exercise, to continue light exercise as tolerated, to carry an epinephrine autoinjector at all times, and to exercise with a partner trained in the use of the epinephrine autoinjector.
In addition, she was instructed to avoid food, NSAIDs, and alcohol intake for at least 4 h prior to exercise.
She was advised to immediately stop the exercise at the first signs of flushing, itching, and hives, self-administer epinephrine, and seek immediate medical assistance.

Our patient followed these instructions and did well for 3 years with occasional reactions, i.e., two attacks on 15th January and 1st April 2021 requiring the use of EpiPen and ER visits, few milder reactions in the first few weeks of June 2021 required antihistamine and no EpiPen or emergency visits and additional episodes on 22nd June 2021, and 7th July 2021 required the use of EpiPen and ER visit.
The patient lives in Qatar, which has a hot and humid climate, especially in the summer months (July to September) and the start of warmer weather begins in March ().

During the summer of 2022, her trigger threshold for anaphylaxis changed markedly, and she began to have frequent episodes of anaphylaxis (10–12 per month) after light exercise and sometimes even after usual daily activities, such as walking for a few minutes from the parking lot to her office and almost all of them required the use of epinephrine autoinjectors; however not all of them attended to ER.
Once, she developed severe anaphylaxis while walking at the airport to the departure gate, collapsed, and was treated with 2 injections of adrenaline in early March 2022.
All anaphylaxis episodes documented in ER records are described in Figure 1.

Because of the high frequency of attacks and the severe impairment in her quality of life, we reassessed the patient by taking a detailed medical history and with new blood work, but we could not identify any new relevant cofactors or comorbidities.

During one episode of anaphylaxis, she experienced chest pain, but the cardiology assessment did not reveal arrhythmia, valvular, myocardial, or coronary artery diseases, and there was no postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome.
A treadmill-based maximal exercise test using the Bruce protocol was carried out, and there was no evidence of ischemia, and she did not develop symptoms of anaphylaxis during the exercise test.

An attempt to increase Levocetirizine to 2 tablets (10 mg) per day was initiated on 20th April 2022, and montelukast 10 mg daily and the recommendation to slow down during walking were not successful in improving the frequency of the attacks.
We then initiated off-label treatment with omalizumab, an anti-IgE antibody, at 300 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks on 4th October 2022.
Seven days after the first injection, our patient reported that she stopped experiencing anaphylaxis attacks and had almost returned to her normal life.
Follow-up at 5 months after initiating omalizumab injections showed no more episodes of anaphylaxis despite regular physical exercise.

pearls: EIA and FDEIA are clinically-based diagnoses that depend on taking meticulous anamnesis to identify the events that precipitate the reaction and the involved cofactors, performing provocation testing, and excluding other mimicking conditions.

Cholinergic urticaria, primary food allergy exacerbated by exercise, cold-induced urticaria/anaphylaxis, mastocytosis and mast cell activation syndrome, cardiovascular events, exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, and postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome should be considered and excluded ().
If EIA is suspected, it must be determined if it is food-dependent (FDEIA) or not, as this is crucial to the prevention of further attacks ().
Our patient was assessed, with negative outcomes, for mimicking conditions and the impact of eating before exercise.

When the patient first presented at our center, the history unequivocally pointed to EIA and excluded mimicking conditions; plus, her attacks were very infrequent, and she responded well to avoidance of strenuous exercise.

src.title: Severe exercise-induced anaphylaxis in a hot and humid area successfully treated with omalizumab: a case report
src.authors: Hassan Mobayed, Maryam Ali Al-Nesf, Karla Robles-Velasco et al.

complaint: A healthy 25-year-old female patient presented with a fractured fixed partial denture (FPD) of teeth 11, 12, and 21.

events.t: A healthy 25-year-old female patient presented with a fractured fixed partial denture (FPD) of teeth 11, 12, and 21.
Clinical examination revealed a fracture of the pontic on the palatal aspect.
A cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) scan was performed, which revealed horizontal alveolar bone resorption at the missing central incisor site.
Rehabilitation of the missing incisor with a dental implant following bone augmentation was decided upon as the treatment of choice.
Following the removal of the FPD, the patient was instructed to rinse with 0.2% chlorhexidine for one minute before beginning the surgical procedure.
The perioral skin was disinfected with a 5% povidone-iodine solution.
Local anesthetic (2% lignocaine with 1:80,000 adrenaline) was used during the surgery.
In addition to releasing incisions, crestal and intrasulcular incisions were made on the labial surfaces of adjacent teeth to obtain access.
A mucoperiosteal flap of full thickness was raised.

The Khoury technique of bone augmentation was used; wherein an autogenous bone block was harvested from the symphysis region of the mandible and stabilized using two microscrews (1.5x10 mm, AK instruments, India) on the labial aspect of the defect.
The generated gap was filled with a combination of autogenous and deproteinized bovine bone xenograft (Bio-Oss; small granules, Geistlich Pharma, Wolhusen, Switzerland).
The flap was sutured and primary closure was obtained.
Postoperative instructions were provided to the patient.
A heat-cured acrylic FPD was cemented post-operatively to serve as a tooth-supported provisional restoration.
After six months of healing, the site was reopened using a modified papilla-sparing incision, and a full-thickness mucoperiosteal flap was raised for implant placement.
The bone demonstrated a horizontal width of 6 mm.
The two microscrews were removed and a 4x11.5 mm implant (Osstem implant TS III, Seoul, Korea) was placed in the central incisor region.
The temporary abutment was positioned at the surgical site following the implant insertion.
To fabricate an interim restoration, the composite resin was incrementally built up over and around the temporary abutment.
To obtain the desired emergence profile, the soft tissue around the interim restoration was molded by relining the composite every two weeks for a period of two months.
A final implant prosthesis was fabricated after the desired emergence profile was achieved.

The gingival contour that was achieved using the prior restoration was transferred to an open-tray impression coping using the technique recommended by Hinds, following which an implant-level impression was made.
The definitive prosthesis was fabricated and inserted.

pearls: Neale and Chee recommended recontouring the tissues using gingivoplasty techniques before fabricating interim restoration.
Consideration must be given to the parameters at each stage, from implant placement to the postoperative phase, to create a harmonious and esthetic emerging profile.

src.title: Customizing the Emergence Profile Around an Immediately Loaded Single Implant in the Esthetic Zone: A Case Report
src.authors: Grazina Fernandes, Ashwin Mysore, Omkar Shetye et al.

complaint: A young 26-year-old patient presented for reconstruction of a missing distal phalange of the ring finger in the Department of Prosthodontics.

events.t: A young 26-year-old patient presented for reconstruction of a missing distal phalange of the ring finger in the Department of Prosthodontics.
During history taking, the patient revealed that he had lost his finger in a bike accident.
He also revealed that he was a musician by profession and played piano.
The sensitive tip of the finger created hindrance while playing piano.
Additionally, the patient was concerned about the aesthetics.
On examination, a healed scar was seen at the base of the amputated ring finger, brown in color with some crusting.
The remaining part of the finger was normal and did not show signs of any infection over the wound.
Various types of materials for the fabrication of the finger prosthesis were presented to the patient.
Considering the cost, the patient opted for heat-cured acrylic material.
The patient was treated with a calm and caring attitude.
He was asked to keep his hand in a relaxed position.
The entire hand was greased with a fine layer of petroleum jelly to allow easy removal of impression material from the finger.
An empty plastic cylinder of the same size as the middle finger was used to make an impression.
Negative casting was made with alginate (Tropicalgin; DPI, India) by placing over and below the amputated finger.
The patient was advised to hold the hand in a normal relaxed position without stretching.
The impression was then poured into the dental stone with utmost care to prevent voids.
The remaining finger on the cast which would contact the finger prosthesis was circumferentially scrapped 1 mm uniformly to get a snug fit.
On retrieval, the positive model of the finger was sculpted in modeling wax.
The wax finger was placed on the amputated finger to evaluate for correct shape and size with adjoining fingers.
After investing and dewaxing, brown color was added in monomer and the clear heat-cured polymer was added to give the prosthesis the look of real skin.
The finger was processed by heat curing with heat-cured acrylic resin using a conventional technique.
On retrieval of the finger prosthesis, the final finishing and polishing were done.
Skin creases were created with a bur.
An additional external painting was performed to get the exact shade in the finished prosthesis.
This was done in front of the patient in natural daylight to gain his approval.
To complete the prosthesis the nail portion was made by mixing pink and clear auto-polymerizing resin to match the patient’s adjacent nail.
The patient was instructed on how to use and maintain the prosthesis.
The patient was advised to clean the prosthesis inside and outside using soap and lukewarm water.
The patient was also advised to keep the prosthesis away from strong solvents to make it last a long time.
The patient was recalled frequently to understand his satisfaction related to comfort, fit, and aesthetics.
The patient was very happy with the function and aesthetics during the three-month, six-month, and one-year follow-ups.

pearls: Fingers play a crucial role in daily tasks, social interaction, as well as aesthetics.
Prosthetic rehabilitation is considered when patients cannot afford it or surgical reconstruction is not possible.

src.title: Acrylic Finger Prosthesis: A Case Report
